title: Throughput tuning deep dive - Atlas Analytics
summary: Redwood SEs walked Atlas Analytics through throughput tuning knobs for their dedicated deployment. Main focus: continuous batching configuration, scheduler parameters (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch), KV cache warm-up and eviction behavior, quantization tradeoffs for latency vs token throughput, and networking considerations for VPC/on-prem. Agreed to run a benchmark with 8xA100 equivalent nodes using mixed-precision quantized model and tuned continuous-batching settings; Redwood to provide a reference script and initial config recommendations.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-15 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Atlas Head ML Infra), Tom Alvarez (Atlas SRE), Hannah Li (Atlas ML Eng), Ethan Park (Atlas Product)
---
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone thanks for making time today, we're gonna jump into throughput tuning, Marcus and Ravi will lead the technical bits. quick callout, we'll capture notes and share the config.
[00:18] Marcus Chen: cool, uh so quick agenda, continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, token budget behavior, kv-cache considerations, quantization impacts, then Q&A and a proposed benchmark plan.
[00:34] Priya Singh: sounds good, our goal is to get 2-3x token throughput without blowing up tail latency; right now on our dedicated pool we see good med latency but severe spikes under burst.
[00:50] Marcus Chen: yep, that's classic batching tradeoff; what you usually want is batching that is adaptive to SLOs. can you remind us of your SLOs?
[01:05] Tom Alvarez: we're targeting 200ms p95 for assistant flows at ~25 concurrent sessions, and a background embedding job that needs sustained 10k tokens/sec.
[01:20] Hannah Li: and a hard token limit per request is 2048, most user calls are ~150 tokens.
[01:28] Marcus Chen: good, so two workloads: short chat-ish requests and long streaming embedding workloads. continuous batching helps for the embedding stream by keeping the GPU fed; for low-latency chat you need small max_num_seqs and aggressive deadline/latency knobs.
[01:45] Ravi Patel: quick note about nomenclature, in Redwood runtime we call the scheduler param max_num_seqs, which controls how many sequences we accumulate before firing a batch; there's also max_tokens_per_batch and an inter-batch timeout (batching_max_delay_ms).
[02:02] Priya Singh: okay, can you walk through recommended starting values for our cluster? we're on 8xA100-ish nodes with 80GB each and using a 13B open model in 4-bit quantization.
[02:18] Marcus Chen: sure. for the chat flow: set max_num_seqs to 8, max_tokens_per_batch to 4096, batching_max_delay_ms to 10ms; that prioritizes latency and will let small batches go out quickly. for the embedding pipeline: bump max_num_seqs to 64, max_tokens_per_batch to 65536, and batching_max_delay_ms up to 50-100ms to allow larger aggregation.
[02:40] Tom Alvarez: won't increasing delay cause p95 issues for chat?
[02:45] Marcus Chen: that's why we split routes; route chat and embeddings to different worker pools or use workload-aware routing. if you must share the same pool, use per-route scheduling profiles with strict deadlines for chat.
[02:58] Hannah Li: you mentioned kv cache warm-up earlier, can you explain how that affects throughput? we've been seeing latency spikes on session resume.
[03:10] Ravi Patel: yep. the KV cache (sometimes transcribed as K V cash in older logs) stores past key/value tensors per session; when warm cache hits are high, per-token cost drops significantly. the problem is cold starts for resumed sessions cause sudden higher compute and inflate p95. recommended: pin hot sessions to workers (sticky session routing) and maintain a small LRU cache with prefetch if you can predict sessions. also tune max_kv_cache_size to avoid evictions during normal load.
[03:40] Priya Singh: what's a realistic max_kv_cache_size for our seq lengths?
[03:45] Marcus Chen: depends on average seq length; if average session length is 150 tokens and you expect 2k concurrent sessions in worst case, that's a lot. start with max_kv_cache_size per-worker at 1000 sessions, monitor memory and eviction rate. we can provide a script to simulate session resume patterns.
[04:05] Ethan Park: any quantization caveats? we're using 4-bit quant, we're seeing some accuracy regressions but large speedups.
[04:14] Marcus Chen: 4-bit (Q4) gives great throughput but can increase compute per-token in some kernels due to dequant/requant steps; for many models it's net win. for low-latency flows, consider mixed mode: use Q4 for background workloads and Q8 or fp16 for chat routes where latency jitter and quality matter. Redwood's runtime supports multiple variants and automatic fallback.
[04:39] Priya Singh: does Redwood automatically fall back to non-quantized variant if quality drops?
[04:44] Ravi Patel: we have a policy-based fallback; you can configure thresholds based on eval metrics and automatic routing to a higher-precision variant. there's also a gradual rollout option.
[04:56] Tom Alvarez: network and VPC considerations — we run in a private VPC with egress restrictions. does maintainining sticky routing or cache pinning require additional networking?
[05:06] Marcus Chen: mostly no; sticky routing is within the Redwood control plane and worker pool, but if you're on private control plane / on-prem there's a small routing metadata channel. if you have strict egress rules, we can provide a private peering setup and run the routing mesh inside your VPC. note that telemetry and certain metrics endpoints are optional to forward.
[05:30] Hannah Li: ok can we talk about scheduler knobs more — specifically max_num_seqs vs max_tokens_per_batch interactions and how deadline scheduling works?
[05:40] Marcus Chen: yes. think of max_num_seqs as sequence-level cap, max_tokens_per_batch as token-budget cap. the scheduler will accept incoming requests and try to form a batch that doesn't exceed either cap. there is also a deadline-based firing: each request has an arrival timestamp and a max_wait_ms; if the deadline expires the batch fires even if below caps. setting batching_max_delay_ms adjusts that.
[06:05] Marcus Chen: key point: for heterogeneous seq lengths, max_tokens_per_batch prevents a large sequence from consuming the budget and starving many short seqs. it's safer to set both caps rather than only one.
[06:18] Priya Singh: our embedding jobs are variable length; sometimes they send 4096-token inputs. won't that cause a batch to be dominated by the long one?
[06:27] Marcus Chen: you can enable sequence pre-sorting or enforce per-route max_request_tokens. we also support splitting very long inputs across micro-batches if model supports it. for embeddings, we often run them in a separate high-throughput pool to avoid interference.
[06:40] Ravi Patel: another lever is token bucketing — group sequences by length to maximize packing efficiency. Redwood runtime supports adaptive bucketing; it reduces padding overhead.
[06:50] Tom Alvarez: what's the impact of batching on tail latency?
[06:55] Marcus Chen: tail latency can increase if you rely on large batching without strict deadlines; set a small latency SLO per route and use per-route max_wait_ms. Also, automatic overflow rules route urgent requests to low-load pools.
[07:10] Hannah Li: do you have telemetry we can monitor to see when batches are firing and cache hit rates?
[07:16] Ravi Patel: yes, the Redwood Console exposes per-route token throughput, batch sizes, average wait time, kv_cache_hit_rate, and eviction counts — you can set alerts on these. we'll share a Grafana dashboard template.
[07:30] Marcus Chen: let's walk through an example config for your chat route. (reads config) route: chat-prod, worker_pool: chat-pool, scheduler: {max_num_seqs: 8, max_tokens_per_batch: 4096, batching_max_delay_ms: 10, max_wait_ms: 20, token_bucketing: true}.
[07:56] Priya Singh: the max_wait_ms and batching_max_delay_ms are distinct?
[08:00] Marcus Chen: yes, batching_max_delay_ms is internal batching loop tick; max_wait_ms is per-request deadline. think of max_wait_ms as SLA bound.
[08:12] Tom Alvarez: can we tune GPU-level knobs too? like kernel selection and max_threads?
[08:18] Marcus Chen: Redwood runtime auto-selects kernels based on model arch and sequence length distribution, but we expose a few advanced flags for kernel preference and workspace sizes. usually unnecessary unless you're squeezing last bits of perf.
[08:31] Hannah Li: we saw a note about max_num_seqs causing OOM in worst-case; how to avoid?
[08:36] Ravi Patel: right — max_num_seqs must consider memory for kv cache and activation memory. set an upper bound based on worker memory headroom; you can set an absolute hard cap on batch memory. also enable early rejection/backpressure when mem pressure crosses threshold.
[08:53] Priya Singh: can Redwood help run load tests that emulate our traffic?
[08:57] Marcus Chen: yes, we provide a benchmark harness; we'll run a 4-hour soak with your traffic profile (chat + embeddings) and produce a report with p50/p95/p99 and recommended scheduler settings.
[09:10] Ethan Park: timeline?
[09:12] Lena Ortiz: we'll provision the harness this week, run baseline next Tue, then one tuned run the following week.
[09:20] Tom Alvarez: on billing — will changing batch sizes affect cost metrics?
[09:25] Marcus Chen: yes, more efficient batching reduces per-token cost. Redwood Console will show token/unit economics per-route so you can see unit cost delta. there's sometimes a small latency tradeoff.
[09:35] Hannah Li: any differences for on-prem vs dedicated cloud?
[09:39] Ravi Patel: on-prem needs you to manage GPU drivers and NCCL versions; we provide a validated stack. network latencies between control plane and workers can increase scheduling jitter if routing is cross-datacenter; we recommend colocating workers. For dedicated cloud, we manage the runtime and can tune autoscaling aggressively.
[09:59] Priya Singh: ok let's detail the benchmark plan and action items.
[10:05] Marcus Chen: plan: 1) baseline run with current config for 2 hours, 2) run tuned config with split pools (chat vs embed) for 2 hours, 3) analyze kv cache hit rates and memory evictions, 4) iterate on max_num_seqs and batching_max_delay_ms. we'll capture traces and kernel-level perf.
[10:25] Lena Ortiz: great, any final Qs?
[10:28] Tom Alvarez: what's the recommended max_num_seqs for fp16 vs Q4?
[10:32] Marcus Chen: for fp16 you can often push higher, maybe 64-128 seqs depending on model and memory; for Q4 the dequant overhead means moderate values, 32-64 is safer. we'll recommend per-model numbers.
[10:45] Priya Singh: thanks, this is very helpful.
[10:48] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone, we'll share the benchmark script, dashboard template, and an initial tuned config by EOD tomorrow.
[10:57] Meeting end

Redwood (Lena): Send initial tuned config and dashboard template by EOD 2025-10-16
Atlas (Priya): Provide traffic profile and sample traces for baseline run
Atlas (Tom): Open firewall/peering tickets if needed for private peering setup
